title: Feeling in Form
subtitle: Spatial research · form-language generation · architectural representation
excerpt: A library and cultural space that translates emotion, perception, events and movement into a field of spatial encounters.
statement: Instead of beginning with rooms, the project begins with feelings and asks what kinds of events a space can invite.
coverAlt: Exploded axonometric drawing of Feeling in Form

sections.label: 01 / Research
sections.title: From emotion to spatial language
body: The original project developed an entity-sense-field framework. Emotional impressions were abstracted into elements, then combined into spatial situations involving enclosure, exposure, encounter, hesitation and movement.
This research became a catalogue of possible relationships rather than a fixed formal vocabulary.

sections.label: 02 / Revision
sections.title: Space, event and movement
body: The later independent revision shifts attention from isolated emotional rooms to the uncertain relationship between architecture and use. Parallel drawing sequences test the building as an object, as an empty spatial condition and as a field occupied by events.

sections.label: 03 / Proposal
sections.title: A fragmented cultural field
body: Courtyards, reading rooms, water, screens, stairs and changing light form a porous composition within the historic district. Routes overlap and spaces remain open to more than one interpretation, allowing visitors to construct their own sequence.

title: Team Workflow Scheduler
subtitle: Java · TCP sockets · concurrency · JavaFX
role: System architecture, protocol, UI and implementation
excerpt: A Java client-server application for managing shared team tasks through a JavaFX desktop client or a command-line interface, with TCP networking and JSON persistence.
statement: A compact exercise in keeping several clients, a shared task lifecycle and persistent state consistent through a deliberately small, legible protocol.

sections.label: 01 / Overview
sections.title: One workflow, several clients
body: The application manages shared team tasks across a JavaFX desktop client and a command-line client for testing raw protocol commands. Both communicate with the same TCP server, so task state must remain predictable even when several users connect at the same time.

Clients send one-line text commands; the server parses each request, updates the shared task list and saves the result to a JSON file. The desktop table refreshes after every operation so the interface stays synchronized with server state.

sections.label: 02 / Capabilities
sections.title: The complete task lifecycle
body: Tasks carry a title, assignee, status, priority and ISO-formatted due time. The application supports the full create, read, update and delete workflow while automatically moving unfinished tasks into an overdue state when their deadline passes.
points: Add tasks with title, assignee, status, priority and due time

sections.label: 03 / Architecture
sections.title: A small distributed application
body: The server listens on port 5050 and creates a dedicated ClientHandler thread for each accepted socket connection. Every handler parses one command and delegates it to a shared SchedulerService, which owns the task lifecycle independently of either interface.

A ConcurrentHashMap provides the shared task collection, with synchronized task mutations and serialized saves protecting critical updates. JSON persistence restores the workspace between sessions, while the service recalculates overdue states whenever tasks are listed or changed.
points: Synchronized task updates and JSON writes

sections.label: 04 / Protocol
sections.title: A readable one-line command format
body: The custom protocol uses a command followed by key-value fields. Its parser accepts quoted values and escaped characters, allowing task titles and assignee names to contain spaces without making the wire format difficult to inspect or test.
points: ADD title="Test 1" assignee="Lee" status=READY priority=1 dueAt=2026-01-01T17:00:00Z

sections.label: 05 / Interfaces
sections.title: A desktop workflow and a direct protocol client
body: The JavaFX client separates add, update and delete actions into dedicated tabs and presents server data in a task table. Network requests run away from the UI thread, then use Platform.runLater to update the interface safely after the server responds.

A command-line client provides a second path into the same server. It keeps the protocol visible during development and makes client-server behaviour easier to inspect without the graphical interface.

sections.label: 06 / Quality
sections.title: Behaviour made testable
body: The project separates domain behaviour from presentation and transport concerns. JUnit 5 tests exercise protocol parsing and formatting as well as adding, listing, updating, deleting, persisting and automatically marking tasks overdue.
Tests use temporary JSON files, keeping service behaviour isolated from the application’s saved task data and making changes safer as the feature set grows.

sections.label: 07 / Run locally
sections.title: Two clients, one server
body: Start SchedulerServer.java first, then run either SchedulerFxClient.java for the desktop interface or SchedulerClient.java for command-line access. Both clients connect to the server on localhost:5050.

title: Vertical City Housing
subtitle: Housing research · massing · circulation · unit planning
excerpt: A high-density housing proposal that turns circulation, landscape and shared programs into a three-dimensional neighbourhood.
statement: The project asks how a residential complex can behave less like a stack of isolated apartments and more like a small city.
coverAlt: Aerial rendering of the Vertical City residential proposal

sections.label: 01 / Premise
sections.title: Housing as a small city
body: Rapid urbanization made high-rise housing an efficient answer to density, but it also produced standardized living, weaker neighbourhood relationships and limited contact with nature. The project uses the idea of the vertical city as a framework for reconnecting private dwellings with collective life.
The research draws from Aldo van Eyck's relationship between the house and the city, Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation and high-density housing precedents in Singapore.

sections.label: 02 / Planning
sections.title: Three courtyards, many elevations
body: The site is divided into three connected courtyard groups. Buildings are cut to form entrances, broken into smaller volumes and varied in height to open views toward Qujiangchi Heritage Park.
Vehicles remain on a semi-peripheral route while pedestrian paths occupy the inner landscape. Commercial programs line the outer edge, and bridges extend the public circulation above ground level.

sections.label: 03 / Living system
sections.title: The corridor becomes an elevated street
body: Single-loaded duplex units reinterpret the interlocking logic of the Marseille apartment. Flexible partitions, cross ventilation, generous balconies and several unit sizes support different households.
Exterior corridors connect to sky bridges, corner commons, roof platforms and double-height voids. These spaces create a continuous network for meeting, playing and moving through the community.

title: BC Travel Guide
subtitle: HTML / CSS / JavaScript · PHP / PDO · MySQL
role: Content structure, responsive interface and full-stack implementation
excerpt: A responsive multi-page travel website combining destination stories, media and an optional subscription backend.
statement: A content-led web project focused on organizing destinations into a clear, responsive browsing experience.
coverAlt: British Columbia travel photography wall used by the website

sections.label: 01 / Content architecture
sections.title: Destinations as stories
body: The site organizes British Columbia destinations through images, written introductions and video. Navigation and page hierarchy keep a growing set of places understandable on both desktop and mobile screens.

Six story cards introduce Vancouver, Vancouver Island, Whistler, the Sea-to-Sky Highway, Stanley Park and Capilano Suspension Bridge. Featured videos, a travel photo wall, contact information and an embedded map broaden the site beyond a simple destination list.

sections.label: 02 / Responsive interface
sections.title: A responsive reading flow
body: HTML and CSS establish the editorial structure, while JavaScript supports interactive behaviour. The layout adapts from large image-led pages to compact mobile reading without hiding essential content.

Anchor navigation moves between Stories, Explore More, Videos and Contact Us. A prominent sign-up action scrolls smoothly to the subscription form, and media cards preserve a consistent hierarchy as the viewport narrows.

sections.label: 03 / Story system
sections.title: One template, six data-driven pages
body: Destination links open one shared story template with a story key in the URL. Vanilla JavaScript reads the query parameter, selects the matching record and renders its title, image, introduction, travel tip, quick facts and related-story links.
Keeping the destination content in a structured JavaScript object avoids duplicating six nearly identical HTML pages and makes the story collection easier to extend.

sections.label: 04 / Subscription backend
sections.title: Optional subscription workflow
body: A PHP and MySQL path extends the static experience with a local subscription workflow, connecting interface design with basic server-side data handling.

The XAMPP setup script creates a subscriptions table containing visitor name, email, favourite article and submission time. A PHP form handler inserts records through a prepared PDO statement, while a separate page retrieves subscribers in reverse chronological order and escapes displayed values.

sections.label: 05 / Hosting boundary
sections.title: A static demo with a local server extension
body: GitHub Pages publishes the responsive frontend, including destination stories and media. Because static hosting cannot execute PHP or connect to MySQL, JavaScript detects unsupported form contexts and directs the user to run the project through XAMPP before submitting.

sections.label: 06 / Run locally
sections.title: Frontend anywhere, subscriptions through XAMPP
body: The published link demonstrates the full frontend. To use subscriptions, place the project in the XAMPP web root, configure the database connection, run php/setup.php once, then open the site at localhost so PHP and MySQL can process and display subscriber records.

title: Car Dealership Manager
subtitle: Java Swing · OOP domain modelling · JSON · JUnit 5
role: Domain modelling, persistence, desktop UI and testing
excerpt: A Java desktop application for managing dealership inventory, customers, brokers and sales through Swing or a console interface, supported by JSON persistence and automated tests.
statement: A desktop application organized around clear domain boundaries rather than a collection of disconnected forms.

sections.label: 01 / Overview
sections.title: A dealership as connected records
body: Vehicles, customers, brokers and sales each have their own behaviour, but the application must connect them without duplicating business rules across screens.
The application gives dealership staff one workspace for adding cars, maintaining inventory status, viewing customer and broker directories, and recording sales that connect all four record types.

sections.label: 02 / Workflow
sections.title: From incoming inventory to completed sale
body: A sale is more than an isolated record: it links a car, buyer, broker and final price, marks the selected vehicle as sold, assigns the customer to the broker and records each change in the event log.
points: Add vehicles with model, year, colour, packages and price
Track six inventory states from creation to sold
Browse inventory, sales, brokers and customers
Record a sale across car, customer and broker IDs
Save or restore the complete dealership workspace

sections.label: 03 / Architecture
sections.title: Domain boundaries before screens
body: The codebase separates model, UI and persistence packages. Dealership acts as the aggregate for cars, brokers, customers and sales; each record type owns its own state while cross-record business rules remain centralized in the dealership model.

The Swing and console entry points operate on the same domain objects, while the Writable contract, JsonReader and JsonWriter keep file serialization outside the interface layer. This organization keeps the model usable independently of either presentation path.

sections.label: 04 / Interface
sections.title: A modular tab-based workspace
body: The Swing interface groups daily operations into focused tabs. Event logging and JSON persistence provide continuity, while the domain model remains usable independently of the interface.

Home handles load and save actions; Inventory presents cars and status editing; Sale links the records needed for a transaction; Directory exposes brokers and customers. A separate console application provides the same core workflow without the graphical layer.

sections.label: 05 / Persistence + events
sections.title: State that survives the session
body: The full dealership aggregate is serialized with org.json to data/dealership.json. The reader reconstructs cars, brokers, customers and sales, while restored car IDs advance the next identifier to reduce collisions after loading.

A singleton EventLog records meaningful model changes such as adding cars, updating status, assigning customers and completing sales. The GUI prints the accumulated log when its window closes, providing a chronological account of the session.

sections.label: 06 / Documentation + quality
sections.title: Design that can be inspected
body: JUnit tests, Checkstyle and a documented UML model make the architecture visible and support disciplined iteration.

Thirty-nine JUnit 5 tests cover the domain model, singleton event log and JSON reader/writer against both general and empty fixtures. The UML diagram records class responsibilities across the tabs, aggregate model, persistence layer and event system.
points: Replace integer car states with a CarStatus enum
Extract common broker and customer fields into Person
Move broker-customer links from IDs to managed object associations

sections.label: 07 / Run locally
sections.title: A Java 11 desktop application
body: Compile the project with JDK 11 or newer and the libraries in lib. Run ui.DealershipUI for the Swing application or ui.Main for the console version; Windows users replace the colon in the classpath with a semicolon.

title: Grid Pursuit: Cheese
subtitle: JavaScript · Canvas API · game state · collision logic
role: Game state, Canvas rendering and interface implementation
excerpt: A 10×10 Canvas game with queued player actions, randomized enemies, traps, walls, scoring and collision detection.
statement: A small game used to make state, timing and collision rules visible through immediate browser interaction.
coverAlt: Complete Grid Pursuit Cheese game interface with board, controls, scoring and status panels

sections.label: 01 / Gameplay
sections.title: A readable grid, unpredictable pressure
body: The player navigates a compact board while enemies move with randomized behaviour. Walls, traps and scoring create tactical choices without obscuring the basic rules.

Mikey begins in the upper-left cell and tries to collect cheese without meeting a kitty. Each cheese increases the score and introduces another kitty; if an enemy reaches the cheese first, the score falls and the target moves.

sections.label: 02 / Turn sequence
sections.title: State changes in a controlled order
body: Queued player actions, enemy movement and collision detection are resolved as explicit stages. Separating these stages prevents one input from producing inconsistent board states.

The player must queue exactly five arrow or trap actions before execution begins. A timer resolves one command every 250 milliseconds; after each action every kitty chooses a random direction, checks the destination and moves only when the cell is valid.
points: Evaluate cheese, trap, wall and kitty collisions

sections.label: 03 / State + collision
sections.title: Coordinates as the shared game model
body: Mikey, cheese, traps, walls and kitties are all represented by grid-aligned coordinates. Kitty and wall collections use coordinate arrays, allowing the same position checks to support random placement, movement blocking and collision outcomes.

Placement routines reject occupied cells and regenerate invalid random positions. Collision rules distinguish direct player-enemy contact, enemies reaching cheese, traps catching one kitty and walls returning an attempted move to its previous cell.

sections.label: 04 / Mechanics
sections.title: Difficulty grows with the score
body: Collecting cheese adds 100 points and introduces a new kitty. A trapped kitty is replaced and awards 250 points, while a kitty reaching the cheese removes 50 points. Optional walls add ten blocked cells and force both player and enemy movement to respect the same spatial constraints.

sections.label: 05 / Rendering
sections.title: Canvas as a compact renderer
body: The Canvas API draws the board and its changing entities efficiently, while surrounding HTML and CSS provide instructions and responsive framing.

Drawing responsibilities are separated into dedicated helpers for the grid, walls, trap, mouse, cheese, kitties and game-over state. Each frame clears the surface and rebuilds the current state from coordinates rather than manipulating many positioned DOM elements.

sections.label: 06 / Controls + testing
sections.title: Game controls that also expose edge cases
body: Arrow keys queue movement and M places a trap. Move Mikey executes a full sequence, Reset regenerates the board, Wall mode adds obstacles, and God Mode prevents capture so movement, scoring and collision behaviour can be inspected for longer sessions.

sections.label: 07 / Run + deployment
sections.title: A dependency-free browser project
body: The game runs directly from index.html with its stylesheet and two JavaScript files: game.js for state and rules, and draw.js for Canvas rendering. The same static structure is published as a playable GitHub Pages demo.

title: Family Tree Database
subtitle: EER modelling · normalization · MySQL · SQL Server
role: Requirements, EER modelling, normalization and SQL implementation
excerpt: A normalized relational model for family relationships, education, employment, addresses, marriages and life events.
statement: The project turns an intuitive but complicated human network into explicit, queryable relationships.

sections.label: 01 / Requirements
sections.title: More than a parent-child tree
body: A useful family-history model must represent people, marriages, addresses, education, employment, achievements and events without flattening them into one oversized table.

The requirements also account for biological and non-biological parenthood, divorce and remarriage, children across different marriages, multiple names, incomplete work histories and attendance at other family members’ life events.

sections.label: 02 / EER model
sections.title: Relationships made explicit
body: An enhanced entity-relationship model identifies stable entities and resolves many-to-many relationships through associative structures. Normalization reduces duplication and protects data integrity.

Person sits at the centre of the model, connected recursively through father, mother and spouse relationships and historically through homes, organizations and achievements. Cardinality and participation rules distinguish required biographical data from optional education, work, marriage and event histories.

sections.label: 03 / Relational mapping
sections.title: Thirteen tables with distinct responsibilities
body: Regular entities become Person, Home, Organization and Achievement tables. Associative history tables resolve many-to-many residence, education, employment and achievement relationships, while recursive parent and spouse tables preserve relationships between people.

Middle names and used names are mapped into separate tables as multivalued attributes. Composite primary keys, unique constraints and foreign-key cascades make duplication and orphaned history records less likely.

sections.label: 04 / Normalization
sections.title: A schema designed against repeated facts
body: The companion normalization study documents how the initial family records are decomposed into stable entities and relationship tables. Separating people, places, organizations and time-bounded histories reduces update anomalies while keeping biographical facts queryable.

sections.label: 05 / SQL implementation
sections.title: One model, two SQL environments
body: The schema is implemented for MySQL and Microsoft SQL Server, demonstrating how a conceptual model is translated across related database systems.

Parallel scripts account for dialect differences such as AUTO_INCREMENT versus IDENTITY(1,1), and TIMESTAMPDIFF versus DATEDIFF. Each platform includes database creation, sample insertion, query and teardown scripts.

sections.label: 06 / Query set
sections.title: Family history as answerable questions
body: Twenty SQL examples test the usefulness of the model through joins, views, updates, deletes, aggregation and unions. They retrieve names and aliases, adults, siblings, parents, adopted children, marriage history, residences, education and work relationships.

The query set moves beyond simple record lookup to questions such as who currently works or studies, who has lived in British Columbia, how many work histories each person has and whether someone later worked for an organization where they studied.
